work.starts: Write the names of the following organism

blocks.en: Groups are made from similar characteristics: plants make their own food; birds have feathers and wings; reptiles have dry scales and lay eggs; mammals have hair or fur and feed their young on milk.

work.starts: Take the seeds of wheat

items.en: One cotyledon (monocot seeds): wheat, rice and maize. The seed does not split into two halves.
Two cotyledons (dicot seeds): pea, bean and gram. The seed splits easily into two halves.

work.starts: pictures of pigeon and butterfly

rows: scales on the wings; a hard outer skeleton
hatch from eggs and look like the parent
hatch as caterpillars that change shape

work.starts: To make a simple microscope

blocks.en: The drop of water on the plastic sheet curves outwards and works as a convex lens. A convex lens bends the light that passes through it, so a tiny object seen through it looks larger. Strong microscopes use glass lenses in the same way to show microorganisms that the eye cannot see.

work.starts: Mix yeast, sugar and water

items.en: The dough with yeast has risen (it is bigger and full of small holes).
Reason: yeast is a living microorganism. It feeds on sugar and gives out carbon dioxide gas, and the gas bubbles make the dough rise.
Sugar was added as food for the yeast. In the other pot there is no yeast, so the dough does not rise.

work.starts: Study the internal structure of bean seed

blocks.en: Two cotyledons. The bean seed splits into two halves; each half is a cotyledon, which stores food for the baby plant. Between them is the embryo (a tiny plumule and radicle). So the bean is a dicot seed.

work.starts: Predict what will happen if we wrap bean seeds

items.en: Prediction: the seeds in wet paper or cotton will also germinate, because they get water and air; a seed needs water, air and a warm temperature, not soil, to start to grow.
In the plastic bag the seeds keep wet, so they germinate; very little air and too much water can make them rot.
In the cup activity: the seed swells, the seed coat splits, the radicle (root) comes out first and grows downwards, then the plumule (shoot) grows upwards and leaves open in the light.

work.starts: Take four test tubes and mark them as A, B, C, D

rows: they have water, air and warmth
water with a layer of oil on top
the oil keeps air away from the seeds
the seeds under water: water only

blocks.en: Conclusion: seeds need water, air and a suitable temperature to germinate.

work.starts: Light a small candle

items.en: The burning candle adds air pollution (smoke and soot).
A black layer appears on the glass: this soot (carbon particles) is formed by the incomplete burning of the wax.
The same happens on a large scale from vehicles, factories and burning rubbish.

work.starts: Can you fill the given table

rows: coughing, asthma and eye trouble; smog; acid rain; harms plants and animals; global warming
diseases such as cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea; fish and water plants die; water is unfit to drink
soil loses its goodness and crops grow badly; rubbish gives bad smells and breeds flies and rats; harms animals that eat it

work.starts: Take two to three spoons of salt

items.en: Can you see the salt in the water? No: it has dissolved (it has mixed with the water and cannot be seen), but the water tastes salty.
After the water has evaporated, the salt is left in the dish. The salt did not change into another substance, so dissolving and evaporating are physical changes.

work.starts: Take an aluminum can

blocks.en: Crushing is a physical change. Only the shape of the can changed; the aluminium did not become a new substance, and it can be melted and made into a can again.

work.starts: Take three glasses of water

rows: they do not dissolve; they settle at the bottom when the water is still (a mixture)
the sugar dissolves and cannot be seen; the water tastes sweet (a solution)
the oil does not mix; it floats on the water as a layer

work.starts: Add a spoon of sugar (solute) in both

blocks.en: The sugar in beaker A (stirred) dissolves quickly. In beaker B (not stirred) it dissolves much more slowly, because the sugar next to it is already sweet and few new water particles reach it. Stirring helps a solute dissolve faster.

work.starts: one cup of hot water (solvent) in beaker A

blocks.en: The sugar dissolves more quickly in beaker A, the hot water. The particles of hot water move faster, so they mix with the sugar sooner: a solute dissolves faster in a hotter solvent.

work.starts: Pour equal quantity of water in five glasses

items.en: The first glass (no drink) holds plain water, so it has no colour.
The second glass (one spoon) has the lightest colour: it is the most dilute solution.
The fifth glass (four spoons) has the darkest colour: it is the most concentrated solution.
More solute in the same amount of water makes a more concentrated solution.

work.starts: Take three test tubes and mark them as A, B, C

rows: boiled water (no air) with oil on top

blocks.en: Iron rusts only when it has both water and air (oxygen). Rusting makes a new reddish-brown substance, so it is a chemical change. Painting, oiling or galvanising iron keeps water and air away.

work.starts: you will form four groups

rows: 1: steel wool burned over a spirit lamp
it glows and turns grey-black (iron oxide) and becomes heavier
2: blue litmus in vinegar, then in lime water
the blue litmus turns red in vinegar (an acid); a red litmus paper is turned blue by lime water (a base)
chemical (a colour change of the indicator)
it burns with a flame and leaves black ash and smoke; it cannot be turned back into paper
after some hours the milk turns into yoghurt: thicker, with a sour taste

blocks.en: In a chemical change a new substance is formed and it cannot easily be changed back; in a physical change only the shape or state changes.

work.starts: Tick (✓) the natural sources of lights

blocks.en: Natural sources of light: the Sun, the stars, lightning and the firefly. The candle and the electric bulb are made by people (artificial sources).

work.starts: Tick (✓) the non luminous objects

blocks.en: Non-luminous objects (they give no light of their own, we see them because they reflect light): the chair, the Moon, the human body and the book page. Luminous: the lighted energy saver, oil lamp, candle, firefly, stars and the Sun.

work.starts: Place a glass full of water on the table in a dark room

items.en: Glass of water: almost all the light passes through and we can see clearly across it: water is transparent.
Glass of milk: some light passes through but we cannot see clearly across it: milk is translucent.
A book or a wooden board: no light passes through; there is a shadow: it is opaque.

work.starts: three identical hard cardboard

blocks.en: The candle flame can be seen only when the three holes and the flame are in one straight line. If one cardboard is moved a little, the flame is hidden. So light travels in a straight line.

work.starts: Place a torch or candle on a table near a wall

items.en: A dark shape of the hand (its shadow) appears on the wall, because the hand is opaque and stops the light, and light travels in straight lines.
Bring the hand near the candle: the shadow on the wall becomes bigger. Move the hand away from the candle (nearer the wall): the shadow becomes smaller and sharper.
Inference: the closer an object is to the light source, the larger its shadow.

work.starts: Place a sound speaker horizontally

blocks.en: The grains jump up and down very fast. Inference: sound is made by vibrations; the cone of the speaker vibrates and makes the grains vibrate.

work.starts: Identify the low and loud sounds

blocks.en: Loud sounds: the lion's roar, the jet plane and thunder. Low (faint) sounds: the bird, the flute and the cat.

work.starts: little bell on the neck of a cattle

blocks.en: Near the bell the sound is loud. When the bell is carried away the sound becomes fainter, and further away it is very low. Inference: the intensity (loudness) of sound decreases as the distance from the source increases.

work.starts: pleasant sounds and (×) for unpleasant

blocks.en: Pleasant (✓): the bird's song and the harmonium. Unpleasant (×): the tractor, the braying donkey, the barking dog and the noise of traffic (noise). What is pleasant can differ from person to person, but harsh and very loud sounds are noise.

work.starts: Suspend two inflated balloons

items.en: Uncharged balloons: they neither attract nor repel; they just hang.
Both rubbed with wool: they get the same (negative) charge and repel each other.
One rubbed with wool and one with plastic: they get opposite charges and attract each other.
Rule: like charges repel, unlike charges attract.

work.starts: Insert a torch bulb in a holder

blocks.en: With the switch ON the circuit is complete, current flows from the cell through the wires and the bulb, and the bulb glows. When the switch is turned OFF the circuit is open (broken), the current stops, and the bulb stops glowing.

work.starts: aluminium foil, a pencil, iron wires, copper wires

rows: aluminium foil, iron wire, copper wire, the graphite of a pencil
eraser (rubber), glass strip, plastic ruler, wood

blocks.en: Metals (and graphite) allow current to pass; non-metals such as rubber, plastic, glass and wood do not.

work.starts: Take a piece of very thin metallic wire

blocks.en: Yes, the thin wire becomes hot and melts, which breaks the circuit. A thin wire has a high resistance, so the current heats it quickly (heating effect of current). A fuse is a thin wire made on this idea: it melts first and cuts the supply when too much current flows, and so protects the appliances.

work.starts: Bring a strong magnet near these things turn by turn

rows: steel pins, iron nails, steel clips

blocks.en: Magnets attract iron and steel (and nickel and cobalt); copper, rubber, wood, stone and plastic are not attracted.

work.starts: Suspend a pencil with the help of a thread

items.en: The pencil stays in whatever direction it was put.
A freely suspended bar magnet always comes to rest along the north-south direction, however many times it is disturbed: one end points to the north (the north pole) and the other to the south.

work.starts: Suspend a bar magnet with the help of a thread such that it can rotate freely

items.en: North pole near north pole: they repel (the suspended magnet turns away).
South pole near south pole: they repel.
North pole near south pole (opposite poles): they attract.
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

work.starts: Remove the magnet placed on the table in the above experiment

blocks.en: The suspended magnet comes to rest along the north-south direction. The Earth behaves like a huge magnet, with its magnetic poles near the geographic poles, and its magnetic field turns the suspended magnet.

work.starts: Wind an insulated copper wire very closely over an iron nail

items.en: Switch OFF: the nail does not attract the pins.
Switch ON: the nail attracts the pins: current in the coil makes the iron nail a magnet (an electromagnet).
Switch OFF again: the pins fall, because the magnetism stops with the current.

work.starts: Take a hard boiled egg

items.en: Three layers: the shell (outside), the white and the yolk (inside).
The thinnest layer is the shell, on the outside; it matches the crust of the Earth.
The biggest part is the white, which matches the mantle.
The yolk is in the middle: it matches the core of the Earth.

work.starts: Take a sample of soil from your school garden

blocks.en: In a garden soil you usually find: small living things such as ants and worms; bits of dead leaves and roots (humus); grains of sand, small stones and minerals; and some moisture that you can feel.

work.starts: Put a sample of soil in a glass bottle or jar

items.en: After two hours the soil settles in layers.
At the bottom: the heaviest particles, stones and gravel, then sand.
Above them: silt and then clay, which keeps the water muddy.
On the surface: dead leaves and bits of plants (humus), which are light and float.

work.starts: Make a drainage hole at the bottom of each cup

blocks.en: Sandy soil drains fastest because its particles are large, with big gaps. Clay has the smallest particles and holds the most water.
